title: Republic, Book 1
author: Plato
source_notes: Greek text: Burnet (OCT) via Perseus. English: Benjamin Jowett 1888 via Perseus.
reading_notes: Book 1 of Plato's Republic. 28 Stephanus sections. Each Greek section aligned with Jowett's English translation for the same section.

lines.original: κατέβην χθὲς εἰς Πειραιᾶ μετὰ Γλαύκωνος τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος προσευξόμενός τε τῇ θεῷ καὶ ἅμα τὴν ἑορτὴν βουλόμενος θεάσασθαι τίνα τρόπον ποιήσουσιν ἅτε νῦν πρῶτον ἄγοντες.
lines.english: I went down yesterday to the Piraeus with Glaucon the son of Ariston, that I might offer up my prayers to the goddess; and also because I wanted to see in what manner they would celebrate the festival, which was a new thing.
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

1. **κατέβην** (καταβαίνω) - 1st sg. aorist indicative active, "I went down"
2. **προσευξόμενος** (προσεύχομαι) - future middle participle, nominative sg. masculine, "intending to pray"
3. **ὡρμημένους** (ὁρμάομαι) - perfect middle/passive participle, accusative pl. masculine, "hastening, setting out"
4. **κρείττους γένεσθε** (κρείττων, γίγνομαι) - comparative adjective + 2nd pl. aorist imperative middle, "become stronger/superior"
5. **πείσωμεν** (πείθω) - 1st pl. aorist subjunctive active, "we should persuade"

**Gloss:**

Socrates narrates his descent to Piraeus with Glaucon to attend a new festival for the goddess, after which Polemarchus's slave detains them as they head home. Polemarchus and his companions playfully challenge Socrates and Glaucon either to prove themselves stronger or to remain, but Socrates suggests a third option:

lines.original: καλὴ μὲν οὖν μοι καὶ ἡ τῶν ἐπιχωρίων πομπὴ ἔδοξεν εἶναι, οὐ μέντοι ἧττον ἐφαίνετο πρέπειν ἣν οἱ Θρᾷκες ἔπεμπον.
lines.english: I was delighted with the procession of the inhabitants; but that of the Thracians was equally, if not more, beautiful.

lines.original: προσευξάμενοι δὲ καὶ θεωρήσαντες ἀπῄμεν πρὸς τὸ ἄστυ.
lines.english: When we had finished our prayers and viewed the spectacle, we turned in the direction of the city;

lines.original: κατιδὼν οὖν πόρρωθεν ἡμᾶς οἴκαδε ὡρμημένους Πολέμαρχος ὁ Κεφάλου ἐκέλευσε δραμόντα τὸν παῖδα περιμεῖναί ἑ κελεῦσαι.
lines.english: and at that instant Polemarchus the son of Cephalus chanced to catch sight of us from a distance as we were starting on our way home, and told his servant to run and bid us wait for him.

lines.original: καί μου ὄπισθεν ὁ παῖς λαβόμενος τοῦ ἱματίου, κελεύει ὑμᾶς, ἔφη, Πολέμαρχος περιμεῖναι.
lines.english: The servant took hold of me by the cloak behind, and said: Polemarchus desires you to wait.

lines.original: καὶ ἐγὼ μετεστράφην τε καὶ ἠρόμην ὅπου αὐτὸς εἴη.
lines.english: I turned round, and asked him where his master was.

lines.original: οὗτος, ἔφη, ὄπισθεν προσέρχεται· ἀλλὰ περιμένετε.
lines.english: There he is, said the youth, coming after you, if you will only wait.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ περιμενοῦμεν, ἦ δʼ ὃς ὁ Γλαύκων.
lines.english: Certainly we will, said Glaucon;

lines.original: καὶ ὀλίγῳ ὕστερον ὅ τε Πολέμαρχος ἧκε καὶ Ἀδείμαντος ὁ τοῦ Γλαύκωνος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Νικήρατος ὁ Νικίου καὶ ἄλλοι τινὲς ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς πομπῆς.
lines.english: and in a few minutes Polemarchus appeared, and with him Adeimantus, Glaucon's brother, Niceratus the son of Nicias, and several others who had been at the procession.

lines.original: ὁ οὖν Πολέμαρχος ἔφη· ὦ Σώκρατες, δοκεῖτέ μοι πρὸς ἄστυ ὡρμῆσθαι ὡς ἀπιόντες.
lines.english: Polemarchus said to me: I perceive, Socrates, that you and your companion are already on your way to the city.

lines.original: οὐ γὰρ κακῶς δοξάζεις, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ.
lines.english: You are not far wrong, I said.

lines.original: ὁρᾷς οὖν ἡμᾶς, ἔφη, ὅσοι ἐσμέν;
lines.english: But do you see, he rejoined, how many we are?

lines.original: πῶς γὰρ οὔ;
lines.english: Of course.

lines.original: ἢ τοίνυν τούτων, ἔφη, κρείττους γένεσθε ἢ μένετʼ αὐτοῦ.
lines.english: And are you stronger than all these? for if not, you will have to remain where you are.

lines.original: οὐκοῦν, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ἔτι ἓν λείπεται, τὸ ἢν πείσωμεν ὑμᾶς ὡς χρὴ ἡμᾶς ἀφεῖναι;
lines.english: May there not be the alternative, I said, that we may persuade you to let us go?

lines.original: ἦ καὶ δύναισθʼ ἄν, ἦ δʼ ὅς, πεῖσαι μὴ ἀκούοντας;
lines.english: But can you persuade us, if we refuse to listen to you? he said.

lines.original: οὐδαμῶς, ἔφη ὁ Γλαύκων.
lines.english: Certainly not, replied Glaucon.

lines.original: ὡς τοίνυν μὴ ἀκουσομένων, οὕτω διανοεῖσθε.
lines.english: Then we are not going to listen; of that you may be assured.

lines.original: ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ καὶ ὁ Ἀδείμαντος, ἆρά γε, ἦ δʼ ὅς, οὐδʼ ἴστε ὅτι λαμπὰς ἔσται πρὸς ἑσπέραν ἀφʼ ἵππων τῇ θεῷ;
lines.english: Adeimantus added: Has no one told you of the torch-race on horseback in honour of the goddess which will take place in the evening?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

1. **λαμπάς** (λαμπάς, -άδος, ἡ) – nominative singular feminine noun: "torch race"
2. **ἀφʼ ἵππων** – preposition ἀπό + genitive plural of ἵππος: "on horseback" (literally "from horses")
3. **διαδώσουσιν** – future active indicative, 3rd plural of διαδίδωμι: "they will hand on/pass along"
4. **παννυχίδα** – accusative singular feminine noun: "all-night festival/vigil"
5. **ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ** – prepositional phrase with genitive: "on the threshold of old age"
6. **ἀπομαραίνονται** – present middle/passive indicative, 3rd plural of ἀπομαραίνω: "wither away, fade"

**Gloss:**

Polemarchus and Adeimantus persuade Socrates to stay for an evening torch race on horseback and an all-night festival honoring the goddess. They proceed to Polemarchus

lines.original: ἀφʼ ἵππων; ἦν δʼ ἐγώ·
lines.english: With horses! I replied:

lines.original: καινόν γε τοῦτο.
lines.english: That is a novelty.

lines.original: λαμπάδια ἔχοντες διαδώσουσιν ἀλλήλοις ἁμιλλώμενοι τοῖς ἵπποις;
lines.english: Will horsemen carry torches and pass them one to another during the race?

lines.original: ἢ πῶς λέγεις;
οὕτως, ἔφη ὁ Πολέμαρχος.
lines.english: Yes, said Polemarchus,

lines.original: καὶ πρός γε παννυχίδα ποιήσουσιν, ἣν ἄξιον θεάσασθαι·
lines.english: and not only so, but a festival will be celebrated at night, which you certainly ought to see.

lines.original: ἐξαναστησόμεθα γὰρ μετὰ τὸ δεῖπνον καὶ τὴν παννυχίδα θεασόμεθα.
lines.english: Let us rise soon after supper and see this festival;

lines.original: καὶ συνεσόμεθά τε πολλοῖς τῶν νέων αὐτόθι καὶ διαλεξόμεθα.
lines.english: there will be a gathering of young men, and we will have a good talk.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ μένετεκαὶ μὴ ἄλλως ποιεῖτε.
lines.english: Stay then, and do not be perverse.

lines.original: καὶ ὁ Γλαύκων, ἔοικεν, ἔφη, μενετέον εἶναι.
lines.english: Glaucon said: I suppose, since you insist, that we must.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ εἰ δοκεῖ, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, οὕτω χρὴ ποιεῖν.
lines.english: Very good, I replied.

lines.original: ἦιμεν οὖν οἴκαδε εἰς τοῦ Πολεμάρχου, καὶ Λυσίαν τε αὐτόθι κατελάβομεν καὶ Εὐθύδημον, τοὺς τοῦ Πολεμάρχου ἀδελφούς, καὶ δὴ καὶ Θρασύμαχον τὸν Καλχηδόνιον καὶ Χαρμαντίδην τὸν Παιανιᾶ καὶ Κλειτοφῶντα τὸν Ἀριστωνύμου·
lines.english: Accordingly we went with Polemarchus to his house; and there we found his brothers Lysias and Euthydemus, and with them Thrasymachus the Chalcedonian, Charmantides the Paeanian, and Cleitophon the son of Aristonymus.

lines.original: ἦν δʼ ἔνδον καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ τοῦ Πολεμάρχου Κέφαλος.
lines.english: There too was Cephalus the father of Polemarchus, whom I had not seen for a long time, and I thought him very much aged.

lines.original: καὶ μάλα πρεσβύτης μοι ἔδοξεν εἶναι· διὰ χρόνου γὰρ καὶἑωράκη αὐτόν.
καθῆστο δὲ ἐστεφανωμένος ἐπί τινος προσκεφαλαίου τε καὶ δίφρου· τεθυκὼς γὰρ ἐτύγχανεν ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ.
lines.english: He was seated on a cushioned chair, and had a garland on his head, for he had been sacrificing in the court;

lines.original: ἐκαθεζόμεθα οὖν παρʼ αὐτόν· ἔκειντο γὰρ δίφροι τινὲς αὐτόθι κύκλῳ.
lines.english: and there were some other chairs in the room arranged in a semicircle, upon which we sat down by him.

lines.original: εὐθὺς οὖν με ἰδὼν ὁ Κέφαλος ἠσπάζετό τε καὶ εἶπεν· ὦ Σώκρατες, οὐ δὲ θαμίζεις ἡμῖν καταβαίνων εἰς τὸν Πειραιᾶ.
lines.english: He saluted me eagerly, and then he said:— You don't come to see me, Socrates, as often as you ought:

lines.original: χρῆν μέντοι.
εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐγὼ ἔτι ἐν δυνάμει ἦ τοῦ ῥᾳδίως πορεύεσθαι πρὸς τὸ ἄστυ, οὐδὲν ἂν σὲ ἔδει δεῦροἰέναι, ἀλλʼ ἡμεῖς ἂν παρὰ σὲ ᾖμεν·
lines.english: If I were still able to go and see you I would not ask you to come to me. But at my age I can hardly get to the city, and therefore you should come oftener to the Piraeus.

lines.original: νῦν δέ σε χρὴ πυκνότερον δεῦρο ἰέναι.
ὡς εὖ ἴσθι ὅτι ἔμοιγε ὅσον αἱ ἄλλαι αἱ κατὰ τὸ σῶμα ἡδοναὶ ἀπομαραίνονται, τοσοῦτον αὔξονται αἱ περὶ τοὺς λόγους ἐπιθυμίαι τε καὶ ἡδοναί.
lines.english: For let me tell you, that the more the pleasures of the body fade away, the greater to me is the pleasure and charm of conversation.

lines.original: μὴ οὖν ἄλλως ποίει, ἀλλὰ τοῖσδέ τε τοῖς νεανίσκοις σύνισθι καὶ δεῦρο παρʼ ἡμᾶς φοίτα ὡς παρὰ φίλους τε καὶ πάνυ οἰκείους.
lines.english: Do not then deny my request, but make our house your resort and keep company with these young men; we are old friends, and you will be quite at home with us.

lines.original: καὶ μήν, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ὦ Κέφαλε, χαίρω γε διαλεγόμενοςτοῖς σφόδρα πρεσβύταις·
lines.english: I replied: There is nothing which for my part I like better, Cephalus, than conversing with aged men;

lines.original: δοκεῖ γάρ μοι χρῆναι παρʼ αὐτῶν πυνθάνεσθαι, ὥσπερ τινὰ ὁδὸν προεληλυθότων ἣν καὶ ἡμᾶς ἴσως δεήσει πορεύεσθαι, ποία τίς ἐστιν, τραχεῖα καὶ χαλεπή, ἢ ῥᾳδία καὶ εὔπορος.
lines.english: for I regard them as travellers who have gone a journey which I too may have to go, and of whom I ought to enquire, whether the way is smooth and easy, or rugged and difficult.

lines.original: καὶ δὴ καὶ σοῦ ἡδέως ἂν πυθοίμην ὅτι σοι φαίνεται τοῦτο, ἐπειδὴ ἐνταῦθα ἤδη εἶ τῆς ἡλικίας ὃ δὴφασιν εἶναι οἱ ποιηταί, πότερον χαλεπὸν τοῦ βίου, ἢ πῶς σὺ αὐτὸ ἐξαγγέλλεις.
lines.english: And this is a question which I should like to ask of you who have arrived at that time which the poets call the 'threshold of old age'—Is life harder towards the end, or what report do you give of it?

lines.original: πῶς, ὦ Σοφόκλεις, ἔχεις πρὸς τἀφροδίσια;
lines.english: How does love suit with age, Sophocles,—are you still the man you were?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **τἀφροδίσια** (τὰ ἀφροδίσια): accusative neuter plural, "sexual matters, sex"
- **συγγίγνεσθαι**: present middle/passive infinitive of συγγίγνομαι, "to have intercourse with"
- **λυττῶντα**: present active participle accusative masculine singular of λυττάω, "raging, mad"
- **ὀλοφύρονται**: present middle indicative 3rd plural of ὀλοφύρομαι, "they lament, bewail"
- **προπηλακίσεις**: accusative feminine plural, "insults, indignities"
- **κόσμιοι**: nominative masculine plural adjective, "orderly, self-controlled"

**Gloss:**

Cephalus recounts a conversation in which someone asked the poet Sophocles whether he could still have sexual relations, to which Sophocles replied that he was glad to have escaped from it as from a mad and savage master. Cephalus uses this anecdote to illustrate that many elderly men wrongly blame old age itself for their misery, when in fact their character (

lines.original: ἔτι οἷός τε εἶ γυναικὶ συγγίγνεσθαι εὐφήμει, ὦ ἄνθρωπε·
lines.english: Peace, he replied;

lines.original: ἁσμενέστατα μέντοι αὐτὸ ἀπέφυγον, ὥσπερ λυττῶντά τινα καὶ ἄγριον δεσπότην ἀποδράς.
lines.english: most gladly have I escaped the thing of which you speak; I feel as if I had escaped from a mad and furious master.

lines.original: ἐγώ σοι, ἔφη, νὴ τὸν Δία ἐρῶ, ὦ Σώκρατες, οἷόν γέ μοι φαίνεται.
lines.english: I will tell you, Socrates, he said, what my own feeling is.

lines.original: πολλάκις γὰρ συνερχόμεθά τινες εἰς ταὐτὸν παραπλησίαν ἡλικίαν ἔχοντες, διασῴζοντες τὴν παλαιὰν παροιμίαν·
lines.english: Men of my age flock together; we are birds of a feather, as the old proverb says;

lines.original: οἱ οὖν πλεῖστοι ἡμῶν ὀλοφύρονται συνιόντες, τὰς ἐν τῇ νεότητι ἡδονὰς ποθοῦντες καὶ ἀναμιμνῃσκόμενοι περί τε τἀφροδίσια καὶ περὶ πότους τε καὶ εὐωχίας καὶ ἄλλʼ ἄττα ἃ τῶν τοιούτων ἔχεται, καὶ ἀγανακτοῦσιν ὡς μεγάλων τινῶν ἀπεστερημένοι καὶ τότε μὲν εὖ ζῶντες, νῦν δὲ οὐδὲ ζῶντες.
lines.english: and at our meetings the tale of my acquaintance commonly is—I cannot eat, I cannot drink; the pleasures of youth and love are fled away: there was a good time once, but now that is gone, and life is no longer life.

lines.original: ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τὰς τῶν οἰκείων προπηλακίσεις τοῦ γήρως ὀδύρονται, καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ δὴ τὸ γῆρας ὑμνοῦσιν ὅσων κακῶν σφίσιν αἴτιον.
lines.english: Some complain of the slights which are put upon them by relations, and they will tell you sadly of how many evils their old age is the cause.

lines.original: ἐμοὶ δὲ δοκοῦσιν, ὦ Σώκρατες, οὗτοι οὐ τὸ αἴτιον αἰτιᾶσθαι.
lines.english: But to me, Socrates, these complainers seem to blame that which is not really in fault.

lines.original: εἰ γὰρ ἦν τοῦτʼ αἴτιον, κἂν ἐγὼ τὰ αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἐπεπόνθη, ἕνεκά γε γήρως, καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι πάντες ὅσοι ἐνταῦθα ἦλθον ἡλικίας.
lines.english: For if old age were the cause, I too being old, and every other old man, would have felt as they do.

lines.original: νῦν δʼ ἔγωγε ἤδη ἐντετύχηκα οὐχ οὕτως ἔχουσιν καὶ ἄλλοις, καὶ δὴ καὶ Σοφοκλεῖ ποτε τῷ ποιητῇ παρεγενόμην ἐρωτωμένῳ ὑπό τινος·
lines.english: But this is not my own experience, nor that of others whom I have known. How well I remember the aged poet Sophocles, when in answer to the question,

lines.original: ἔφη,;
καὶ ὅς,ἔφη,
εὖ οὖν μοι καὶ τότε ἔδοξεν ἐκεῖνος εἰπεῖν, καὶ νῦν οὐχ ἧττον.
lines.english: His words have often occurred to my mind since, and they seem as good to me now as at the time when he uttered them.

lines.original: παντάπασι γὰρ τῶν γε τοιούτων ἐν τῷ γήρᾳ πολλὴ εἰρήνη γίγνεται καὶ ἐλευθερία·
lines.english: For certainly old age has a great sense of calm and freedom;

lines.original: ἐπειδὰν αἱ ἐπιθυμίαι παύσωνται κατατείνουσαι καὶ χαλάσωσιν, παντάπασιν τὸ τοῦ Σοφοκλέους γίγνεται,δεσποτῶν πάνυ πολλῶν ἐστι καὶ μαινομένων ἀπηλλάχθαι.
lines.english: when the passions relax their hold, then, as Sophocles says, we are freed from the grasp not of one mad master only, but of many.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ καὶ τούτων πέρι καὶ τῶν γε πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους μία τις αἰτία ἐστίν, οὐ τὸ γῆρας, ὦ Σώκρατες, ἀλλʼ ὁ τρόπος τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
lines.english: The truth is, Socrates, that these regrets, and also the complaints about relations, are to be attributed to the same cause, which is not old age, but men's characters and tempers;

lines.original: ἂν μὲν γὰρ κόσμιοι καὶ εὔκολοι ὦσιν, καὶ τὸ γῆρας μετρίως ἐστὶν ἐπίπονον·
lines.english: for he who is of a calm and happy nature will hardly feel the pressure of age,

lines.original: εἰ δὲ μή, καὶ γῆρας, ὦ Σώκρατες, καὶ νεότης χαλεπὴ τῷ τοιούτῳ συμβαίνει.
lines.english: but to him who is of an opposite disposition youth and age are equally a burden.

lines.original: καὶ ἐγὼ ἀγασθεὶς αὐτοῦ εἰπόντος ταῦτα, βουλόμενος ἔτιλέγειν αὐτὸν ἐκίνουν καὶ εἶπον·
lines.english: I listened in admiration, and wanting to draw him out, that he might go on—

lines.original: ὦ Κέφαλε, οἶμαί σου τοὺς πολλούς, ὅταν ταῦτα λέγῃς, οὐκ ἀποδέχεσθαι ἀλλʼ ἡγεῖσθαί σε ῥᾳδίως τὸ γῆρας φέρειν οὐ διὰ τὸν τρόπον ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ πολλὴν οὐσίαν κεκτῆσθαι·
lines.english: Yes, Cephalus, I said: but I rather suspect that people in general are not convinced by you when you speak thus; they think that old age sits lightly upon you, not because of your happy disposition, but because you are rich,

lines.original: τοῖς γὰρ πλουσίοις πολλὰ παραμύθιά φασιν εἶναι.
lines.english: and wealth is well known to be a great comforter.

lines.original: ἀληθῆ, ἔφη, λέγεις· οὐ γὰρ ἀποδέχονται.
lines.english: You are right, he replied; they are not convinced:
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **ἀποδέχονται** (3rd pl. pres. mid. indic. of ἀποδέχομαι): "they accept, approve"
- **λοιδορουμένῳ** (pres. mid. participle, dat. sg. masc.): "to the one reviling/insulting"
- **ἐπεκτησάμην** (1st sg. aor. mid. indic. of ἐπικτάομαι): "I acquired in addition"
- **ἀγαπῶσιν** (3rd pl. pres. act. indic. of ἀγαπάω): "they love, cherish"
- **εἰσέρχεται** (3rd sg. pres. mid. indic. of εἰσέρχομαι): "enters into, comes upon"
- **ἀναλογίζεται** (3rd sg. pres. mid. indic. of ἀναλογίζομαι): "he reckons up, calculates"

**Gloss:**

Cephalus affirms that wealth matters less than character, illustrating with

lines.original: καὶ λέγουσι μέν τι, οὐ μέντοι γε ὅσον οἴονται· ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῦ Θεμιστοκλέους εὖ ἔχει, ὃς τῷ Σεριφίῳ λοιδορουμένῳ καὶ λέγοντι ὅτι οὐ δι' αὑτὸν ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν πόλιν εὐδοκιμοῖ, ἀπεκρίνατο ὅτι οὔτ' ἂν αὐτὸς Σερίφιος ὢν ὀνομαστὸς ἐγένετο οὔτ' ἐκεῖνος Ἀθηναῖος.
lines.english: and there is something in what they say; not, however, so much as they imagine. I might answer them as Themistocles answered the Seriphian who was abusing him and saying that he was famous, not for his own merits but because he was an Athenian: 'If you had been a native of my country or I of yours, neither of us would have been famous.'

lines.original: καὶ τοῖς δὴ μὴ πλουσίοις, χαλεπῶς δὲ τὸ γῆρας φέρουσιν, εὖ ἔχει ὁ αὐτὸς λόγος, ὅτι οὔτ' ἂν ὁ ἐπιεικὴς πάνυ τι ῥᾳδίως γῆρας μετὰ πενίας ἐνέγκοι οὔθ' ὁ μὴ ἐπιεικὴς πλουτήσας εὔκολός ποτ' ἂν ἑαυτῷ γένοιτο.
lines.english: And to those who are not rich and are impatient of old age, the same reply may be made; for to the good poor man old age cannot be a light burden, nor can a bad rich man ever have peace with himself.

lines.original: πότερον δέ, ἦν δ' ἐγώ, ὦ Κέφαλε, ὧν κέκτησαι τὰ πλείω παρέλαβες ἢ ἐπεκτήσω;
lines.english: May I ask, Cephalus, whether your fortune was for the most part inherited or acquired by you?

lines.original: ποῖ' ἐπεκτησάμην, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες; μέσος τις γέγονα χρηματιστὴς τοῦ τε πάππου καὶ τοῦ πατρός.
lines.english: Acquired! Socrates; do you want to know how much I acquired? In the art of making money I have been midway between my father and grandfather:

lines.original: ὁ μὲν γὰρ πάππος τε καὶ ὁμώνυμος ἐμοὶ σχεδόν τι ὅσην ἐγὼ νῦν οὐσίαν κέκτημαι παραλαβὼν πολλάκις τοσαύτην ἐποίησεν, Λυσανίας δὲ ὁ πατὴρ ἔτι ἐλάττω αὐτὴν ἐποίησε τῆς νῦν οὔσης· ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγαπῶ ἐὰν μὴ ἐλάττω καταλίπω τούτοισιν, ἀλλὰ βραχεῖ γέ τινι πλείω ἢ παρέλαβον.
lines.english: for my grandfather, whose name I bear, doubled and trebled the value of his patrimony, that which he inherited being much what I possess now; but my father Lysanias reduced the property below what it is at present: and I shall be satisfied if I leave to these my sons not less but a little more than I received.

lines.original: οὗ τοι ἕνεκα ἠρόμην, ἦν δ' ἐγώ, ὅτι μοι ἔδοξας οὐ σφόδρα ἀγαπᾶν τὰ χρήματα, τοῦτο δὲ ποιοῦσιν ὡς τὸ πολὺ οἳ ἂν μὴ αὐτοὶ κτήσωνται· οἱ δὲ κτησάμενοι διπλῇ ἢ οἱ ἄλλοι ἀσπάζονται αὐτά.
lines.english: That was why I asked you the question, I replied, because I see that you are indifferent about money, which is a characteristic rather of those who have inherited their fortunes than of those who have acquired them; the makers of fortunes have a second love of money as a creation of their own, resembling the affection of authors for their own poems, or of parents for their children, besides that natural love of it for the sake of use and profit which is common to them and all men.

lines.original: ὥσπερ γὰρ οἱ ποιηταὶ τὰ αὑτῶν ποιήματα καὶ οἱ πατέρες τοὺς παῖδας ἀγαπῶσιν, ταύτῃ τε δὴ καὶ οἱ χρηματισάμενοι περὶ τὰ χρήματα σπουδάζουσιν ὡς ἔργον ἑαυτῶν, καὶ κατὰ τὴν χρείαν ᾗπερ οἱ ἄλλοι.
lines.english: And hence they are very bad company, for they can talk about nothing but the praises of wealth.

lines.original: χαλεποὶ οὖν καὶ συγγενέσθαι εἰσίν, οὐδὲν ἐθέλοντες ἐπαινεῖν ἀλλ' ἢ τὸν πλοῦτον.
ἀληθῆ, ἔφη, λέγεις.
lines.english: That is true, he said.

lines.original: πάνυ μὲν οὖν, ἦν δ' ἐγώ.
lines.english: Yes, that is very true, but may I ask another question?

lines.original: ἀλλά μοι ἔτι τοσόνδε εἰπέ· τί μέγιστον οἴει ἀγαθὸν ἀπολελαυκέναι τοῦ πολλὴν οὐσίαν κεκτῆσθαι;
lines.english: What do you consider to be the greatest blessing which you have reaped from your wealth?

lines.original: ὅ, ἦ δ' ὅς, ἴσως οὐκ ἂν πολλοὺς πείσαιμι λέγων.
lines.english: One, he said, of which I could not expect easily to convince others.

lines.original: εὖ γὰρ ἴσθι, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες, ὅτι, ἐπειδάν τις ἐγγὺς ᾖ τοῦ οἴεσθαι τελευτήσειν, εἰσέρχεται αὐτῷ δέος καὶ φροντὶς περὶ ὧν ἔμπροσθεν οὐκ εἰσῄει.
lines.english: For let me tell you, Socrates, that when a man thinks himself to be near death, fears and cares enter into his mind which he never had before;

lines.original: οἵ τε γὰρ λεγόμενοι μῦθοι περὶ τῶν ἐν Ἅιδου, ὡς τὸν ἐνθάδε ἀδικήσαντα δεῖ ἐκεῖ διδόναι δίκην, καταγελώμενοι τέως, τότε δὴ στρέφουσιν αὐτοῦ τὴν ψυχὴν μὴ ἀληθεῖς ὦσιν·
lines.english: the tales of a world below and the punishment which is exacted there of deeds done here were once a laughing matter to him, but now he is tormented with the thought that they may be true:

lines.original: καὶ αὐτός—ἤτοι ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ γήρως ἀσθενείας ἢ καὶ ὥσπερ ἤδη ἐγγυτέρω ὢν τῶν ἐκεῖ μᾶλλόν τι καθορᾷ αὐτά—ὑποψίας δ' οὖν καὶ δείματος μεστὸς γίγνεται καὶ ἀναλογίζεται ἤδη καὶ σκοπεῖ εἴ τινά τι ἠδίκησεν.
lines.english: either from the weakness of age, or because he is now drawing nearer to that other place, he has a clearer view of these things; suspicions and alarms crowd thickly upon him, and he begins to reflect and consider what wrongs he has done to others.

lines.original: γηροτρόφος γλυκεῖά οἱ καρδίαν ἀτάλλοισα γηροτρόφος συναορεῖ ἐλπὶς ἃ μάλιστα θνατῶν πολύστροφον γνώμαν κυβερνᾷ.
lines.english: 'Hope,' he says, 'cherishes the soul of him who lives in justice and holiness, and is the nurse of his age and the companion of his journey;—hope which is mightiest to sway the restless soul of man.'
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **γηροτρόφος** (nom. fem. sing., adjective): "nourishing old age," "cherishing old age"
- **ἀτάλλοισα** (nom. fem. sing., present participle): "fostering," "cherishing"
- **συναορεῖ** (3rd sing. pres. indic.): "accompanies," "attends"
- **κυβερνᾷ** (3rd sing. pres. indic.): "steers," "governs"
- **ἐλπίς** (nom. fem. sing.): "hope," "expectation"
- **ἀποδιδόναι** (pres. act. infin.): "to give back," "to restore"

**Gloss:**

Cephalus cites Pindar on how hope that nourishes old age accompanies and governs the mortal mind, then contrasts the man conscious of many injustices (who lives with dread, like children waking from nightmares) with the just man who enjoys good hope. He argues that wealth's chief value for the decent man is enabling him to avoid deception and debt, particularly to gods and men, before departing to the afterlife

lines.original: ὁ μὲν οὖν εὑρίσκων ἑαυτοῦ ἐν τῷ βίῳ πολλὰ ἀδικήματα καὶ ἐκ τῶν ὕπνων, ὥσπερ οἱ παῖδες, θαμὰ ἐγειρόμενος δειμαίνει καὶ ζῇ μετὰ κακῆς ἐλπίδος·
lines.english: And when he finds that the sum of his transgressions is great he will many a time like a child start up in his sleep for fear, and he is filled with dark forebodings.

lines.original: τῷ δὲ μηδὲν ἑαυτῷ ἄδικον συνειδότι ἡδεῖα ἐλπὶς ἀεὶ πάρεστι καὶ ἀγαθὴ, ὡς καὶ Πίνδαρος λέγει.
lines.english: But to him who is conscious of no sin, sweet hope, as Pindar charmingly says, is the kind nurse of his age:

lines.original: χαριέντως γάρ τοι, ὦ Σώκρατες, τοῦτʼ ἐκεῖνος εἶπεν, ὅτι ὃς ἂν δικαίως καὶ ὁσίως τὸν βίον διαγάγῃ,
lines.english: How admirable are his words!

lines.original: εὖ οὖν λέγει θαυμαστῶς ὡς σφόδρα.
lines.english: How admirable are his words!

lines.original: πρὸς δὴ τοῦτʼ ἔγωγε τίθημι τὴν τῶν χρημάτων κτῆσιν πλείστου ἀξίαν εἶναι, οὔτι παντὶ ἀνδρὶ ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπιεικεῖ καὶ κοσμίῳ.
lines.english: And the great blessing of riches, I do not say to every man, but to a good man, is, that he has had no occasion to deceive or to defraud others, either intentionally or unintentionally;

lines.original: τὸ γὰρ μηδὲ ἄκοντά τινα ἐξαπατῆσαι ἢ ψεύσασθαι, μηδʼ αὖ ὀφείλοντα ἢ θεῷ θυσίας τινὰς ἢ ἀνθρώπῳ χρήματα ἔπειτα ἐκεῖσε ἀπιέναι δεδιότα, μέγα μέρος εἰς τοῦτο ἡ τῶν χρημάτων κτῆσις συμβάλλεται.
lines.english: and when he departs to the world below he is not in any apprehension about offerings due to the gods or debts which he owes to men. Now to this peace of mind the possession of wealth greatly contributes;

lines.original: ἔχει δὲ καὶ ἄλλας χρείας πολλάς·
lines.english: and therefore I say, that, setting one thing against another, of the many advantages which wealth has to give,

lines.original: ἀλλὰ ἕν γε ἀνθʼ ἑνὸς οὐκ ἐλάχιστον ἔγωγε θείην ἂν εἰς τοῦτο ἀνδρὶ νοῦν ἔχοντι, ὦ Σώκρατες, πλοῦτον χρησιμώτατον εἶναι.
lines.english: to a man of sense this is in my opinion the greatest.

lines.original: παγκάλως, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, λέγεις, ὦ Κέφαλε.
lines.english: Well said, Cephalus, I replied;

lines.original: τοῦτο δʼ αὐτό, τὴν δικαιοσύνην, πότερα τὴν ἀλήθειαν αὐτὸ φήσομεν εἶναι ἁπλῶς οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἀποδιδόναι ἄν τίς τι παρά του λάβῃ, ἢ καὶ αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἔστιν ἐνίοτε μὲν δικαίως, ἐνίοτε δὲ ἀδίκως ποιεῖν;
lines.english: but as concerning justice, what is it?—to speak the truth and to pay your debts—no more than this? And even to this are there not exceptions?

lines.original: οἷον τοιόνδε λέγω· πᾶς ἄν που εἴποι, εἴ τις λάβοι παρὰ φίλου ἀνδρὸς σωφρονοῦντος ὅπλα, εἰ μανεὶς ἀπαιτοῖ, ὅτι οὔτε χρὴ τὰ τοιαῦτα ἀποδιδόναι, οὔτε δίκαιος ἂν εἴη ὁ ἀποδιδούς, οὐδʼ αὖ πρὸς τὸν οὕτως ἔχοντα πάντα ἐθέλων τἀληθῆ λέγειν.
lines.english: Suppose that a friend when in his right mind has deposited arms with me and he asks for them when he is not in his right mind, ought I to give them back to him? No one would say that I ought or that I should be right in doing so, any more than they would say that I ought always to speak the truth to one who is in his condition.

lines.original: ὀρθῶς, ἔφη, λέγεις.
lines.english: You are quite right, he replied.

lines.original: οὐκ ἄρα οὗτος ὅρος ἐστὶν δικαιοσύνης, ἀληθῆ τε λέγειν καὶ ἃ ἂν λάβῃ τις ἀποδιδόναι.
lines.english: But then, I said, speaking the truth and paying your debts is not a correct definition of justice.

lines.original: πάνυ μὲν οὖν, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες, ὑπολαβὼν ὁ Πολέμαρχος, εἴπερ γέ τι χρὴ Σιμωνίδῃ πείθεσθαι.
lines.english: Quite correct, Socrates, if Simonides is to be believed, said Polemarchus interposing.

lines.original: καὶ μέντοι, ἔφη ὁ Κέφαλος, καὶ παραδίδωμι ὑμῖν τὸν λόγον·
lines.english: I fear, said Cephalus, that I must go now, for I have to look after the sacrifices, and I hand over the argument to Polemarchus and the company.

lines.original: δεῖ γάρ με ἤδη τῶν ἱερῶν ἐπιμεληθῆναι.
lines.english: I fear, said Cephalus, that I must go now, for I have to look after the sacrifices, and I hand over the argument to Polemarchus and the company.

lines.original: οὐκοῦν, ἔφη, ἐγώ, ὁ Πολέμαρχος, τῶν γε σῶν κληρονόμος;
lines.english: Is not Polemarchus your heir? I said.

lines.original: πάνυ γε, ἦ δʼ ὃς γελάσας, καὶ ἅμα ᾔει πρὸς τὰ ἱερά.
lines.english: To be sure, he answered, and went away laughing to the sacrifices.

lines.original: λέγε δή, εἶπον ἐγώ, σὺ ὁ τοῦ λόγου κληρονόμος, τί φῂς τὸν Σιμωνίδην λέγοντα ὀρθῶς λέγειν περὶ δικαιοσύνης;
lines.english: Tell me then, O thou heir of the argument, what did Simonides say, and according to you truly say, about justice?

lines.original: ὅτι, ἦ δʼ ὅς, τὸ τὰ ὀφειλόμενα ἑκάστῳ ἀποδιδόναι δίκαιόν ἐστι·
lines.english: He said that the repayment of a debt is just,

lines.original: τοῦτο λέγων δοκεῖ ἔμοιγε καλῶς λέγειν.
lines.english: and in saying so he appears to me to be right.

lines.original: ὦ Σιμωνίδη, ἡ τίσιν οὖν τί ἀποδιδοῦσα ὀφειλόμενον καὶ προσῆκον τέχνη ἰατρικὴ καλεῖται;
lines.english: By heaven! I replied; and if we asked him what due or proper thing is given by medicine, and to whom, what answer do you think that he would make to us?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**
- *ἀποδιδοῦσα* (present active participle, feminine nominative singular, from ἀποδίδωμι): "giving back, rendering"
- *ὀφειλόμενον* (present passive participle, neuter accusative singular, from ὀφείλω): "what is owed, due"
- *προσῆκον* (present active participle, neuter accusative singular, from προσήκω): "what is fitting, appropriate"
- *ἠινίξατο* (aorist middle indicative, 3rd singular, from αἰνίσσομαι): "spoke in riddles, hinted at"
- *ἄχρηστος* (adjective, nominative singular): "useless"

**Gloss:**
Socrates questions Polemarchus about Simonides' definition of justice as "rendering what is owed," using analogies to medicine and cooking to establish that each craft renders what is fitting to specific recipients. The discussion probes whether justice, defined as benefiting friends and harming enemies, operates only in contexts of conflict (like a doctor treating the sick) or has utility in peacetime as well, with Polemarchus forced to admit Si

lines.original: ἀλλὰ μέντοι, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, Σιμωνίδῃ γε οὐ ῥᾴδιον ἀπιστεῖν—σοφὸς γὰρ καὶ θεῖος ἀνήρ—τοῦτο μέντοι ὅτι ποτὲ λέγει, σὺ μέν, ὦ Πολέμαρχε, ἴσως γιγνώσκεις, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγνοῶ·
lines.english: I should be sorry to doubt the word of such a wise and inspired man, but his meaning, though probably clear to you, is the reverse of clear to me.

lines.original: δῆλον γὰρ ὅτι οὐ τοῦτο λέγει, ὅπερ ἄρτι ἐλέγομεν, τό τινος παρακαταθεμένου τι ὁτῳοῦν μὴ σωφρόνως ἀπαιτοῦντι ἀποδιδόναι.
lines.english: For he certainly does not mean, as we were just now saying, that I ought to return a deposit of arms or of anything else to one who asks for it when he is not in his right senses; and yet a deposit cannot be denied to be a debt.

lines.original: καίτοι γε ὀφειλόμενόν πού ἐστιν τοῦτο ὃ παρακατέθετο· ἦ γάρ;
lines.english: True.

lines.original: ναί.
ἀποδοτέον δέ γε οὐδʼ ὁπωστιοῦν τότε ὁπότε τις μὴ σωφρόνως ἀπαιτοῖ;
lines.english: Then when the person who asks me is not in his right mind I am by no means to make the return?

lines.original: ἀληθῆ, ἦ δʼ ὅς.
lines.english: Certainly not.

lines.original: ἄλλο δή τι ἢ τὸ τοιοῦτον, ὡς ἔοικεν, λέγει Σιμωνίδης τὸ τὰ ὀφειλόμενα δίκαιον εἶναι ἀποδιδόναι.
lines.english: When Simonides said that the repayment of a debt was justice, he did not mean to include that case?

lines.original: ἄλλο μέντοι νὴ Δίʼ, ἔφη·
lines.english: Certainly not;

lines.original: τοῖς γὰρ φίλοις οἴεται ὀφείλειν τοὺς φίλους ἀγαθὸν μέν τι δρᾶν, κακὸν δὲ μηδέν.
lines.english: for he thinks that a friend ought always to do good to a friend and never evil.

lines.original: μανθάνω, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ—ὅτι οὐ τὰ ὀφειλόμενα ἀποδίδωσιν ὃς ἄν τῳ χρυσίον ἀποδῷ παρακαταθεμένῳ, ἐάνπερ ἡ ἀπόδοσις καὶ ἡ λῆψις βλαβερὰ γίγνηται, φίλοι δὲ ὦσιν ὅ τε ἀπολαμβάνων καὶ ὁ ἀποδιδούς—οὐχ οὕτω λέγειν φῂς τὸν Σιμωνίδην;
lines.english: You mean that the return of a deposit of gold which is to the injury of the receiver, if the two parties are friends, is not the repayment of a debt,—that is what you would imagine him to say?

lines.original: πάνυ μὲν οὖν.
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: τί δέ;
τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἀποδοτέον ὅτι ἂν τύχῃ ὀφειλόμενον;
lines.english: And are enemies also to receive what we owe to them?

lines.original: παντάπασι μὲν οὖν, ἔφη, ὅ γε ὀφείλεται αὐτοῖς, ὀφείλεται δέ γε οἶμαι παρά γε τοῦ ἐχθροῦ τῷ ἐχθρῷ ὅπερ καὶ προσήκει, κακόν τι.
lines.english: To be sure, he said, they are to receive what we owe them, and an enemy, as I take it, owes to an enemy that which is due or proper to him—that is to say, evil.

lines.original: ἠινίξατο ἄρα, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ὡς ἔοικεν, ὁ Σιμωνίδης ποιητικῶς τὸ δίκαιον ὃ εἴη.
lines.english: Simonides, then, after the manner of poets, would seem to have spoken darkly of the nature of justice;

lines.original: διενοεῖτο μὲν γάρ, ὡς φαίνεται, ὅτι τοῦτʼ εἴη δίκαιον, τὸ προσῆκον ἑκάστῳ ἀποδιδόναι, τοῦτο δὲ ὠνόμασεν ὀφειλόμενον.
lines.english: for he really meant to say that justice is the giving to each man what is proper to him, and this he termed a debt.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ τί οἴει;
lines.english: That must have been his meaning, he said.

lines.original: ἔφη.
ὦ πρὸς Διός, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, εἰ οὖν τις αὐτὸν ἤρετο· τί ἂν οἴει ἡμῖν αὐτὸν ἀποκρίνασθαι;
δῆλον ὅτι, ἔφη, ἡ σώμασιν φάρμακά τε καὶ σιτία καὶ ποτά.
lines.english: He would surely reply that medicine gives drugs and meat and drink to human bodies.

lines.original: ἡ δὲ τίσιν τί ἀποδιδοῦσα ὀφειλόμενον καὶ προσῆκον τέχνη μαγειρικὴ καλεῖται;
lines.english: And what due or proper thing is given by cookery, and to what?

lines.original: ἡ τοῖς ὄψοις τὰ ἡδύσματα.
lines.english: Seasoning to food.

lines.original: εἶεν·
ἡ οὖν δὴ τίσιν τί ἀποδιδοῦσα τέχνη δικαιοσύνη ἂν καλοῖτο;
lines.english: And what is that which justice gives, and to whom?

lines.original: εἰ μέν τι, ἔφη, δεῖ ἀκολουθεῖν, ὦ Σώκρατες, τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν εἰρημένοις, ἡ τοῖς φίλοις τε καὶ ἐχθροῖς ὠφελίας τε καὶ βλάβας ἀποδιδοῦσα.
lines.english: If, Socrates, we are to be guided at all by the analogy of the preceding instances, then justice is the art which gives good to friends and evil to enemies.

lines.original: τὸ τοὺς φίλους ἄρα εὖ ποιεῖν καὶ τοὺς ἐχθροὺς κακῶς δικαιοσύνην λέγει;
lines.english: That is his meaning then?

lines.original: δοκεῖ μοι.
lines.english: I think so.

lines.original: τίς οὖν δυνατώτατος κάμνοντας φίλους εὖ ποιεῖν καὶ ἐχθροὺς κακῶς πρὸς νόσον καὶ ὑγίειαν;
lines.english: And who is best able to do good to his friends and evil to his enemies in time of sickness?

lines.original: ἰατρός.
lines.english: The physician.

lines.original: τίς δὲ πλέοντας πρὸς τὸν τῆς θαλάττης κίνδυνον;
lines.english: Or when they are on a voyage, amid the perils of the sea?

lines.original: κυβερνήτης.
lines.english: The pilot.

lines.original: τί δὲ ὁ δίκαιος;
ἐν τίνι πράξει καὶ πρὸς τί ἔργον δυνατώτατος φίλους ὠφελεῖν καὶ ἐχθροὺς βλάπτειν;
lines.english: And in what sort of actions or with a view to what result is the just man most able to do harm to his enemy and good to his friend?

lines.original: ἐν τῷ προσπολεμεῖν καὶ ἐν τῷ συμμαχεῖν, ἔμοιγε δοκεῖ.
lines.english: In going to war against the one and in making alliances with the other.

lines.original: εἶεν·
μὴ κάμνουσί γε μήν, ὦ φίλε Πολέμαρχε, ἰατρὸς ἄχρηστος.
lines.english: But when a man is well, my dear Polemarchus, there is no need of a physician?

lines.original: ἀληθῆ.
lines.english: No.

lines.original: καὶ μὴ πλέουσι δὴ κυβερνήτης.
lines.english: And he who is not on a voyage has no need of a pilot?

lines.original: ναί.
lines.english: No.

lines.original: ἆρα καὶ τοῖς μὴ πολεμοῦσιν ὁ δίκαιος ἄχρηστος;
lines.english: Then in time of peace justice will be of no use?

lines.original: οὐ πάνυ μοι δοκεῖ τοῦτο.
lines.english: I am very far from thinking so.

lines.original: χρήσιμον ἄρα καὶ ἐν εἰρήνῃ δικαιοσύνη;
lines.english: You think that justice may be of use in peace as well as in war? Yes.

lines.original: χρήσιμον.
lines.english: Like husbandry for the acquisition of corn?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**
- **συμβόλαια** (neuter plural accusative): "contracts, dealings" – from συμβόλαιον
- **κοινωνήματα** (neuter plural nominative/accusative): "partnerships, associations" – from κοινώνημα
- **πεττευτικός** (adjective, nominative masculine singular): "skilled in board-games" – from πεττεύω
- **παρακαταθέσθαι** (aorist middle infinitive): "to deposit (for safekeeping)" – from παρακατατίθημι
- **ἄχρηστος/-ον** (adjective): "useless, unprofitable"

**Gloss:**
Socrates systematically undermines Polemarchus's claim that justice is useful in "contracts" (συμβόλαια) or "partnerships" (κοινωνήματα) by showing that in every practical partnership—whether board-games, building, or monetary transactions—the relevant specialist (πεττευτικός, οἰκοδομικός, etc.) is more useful than the just person. Justice proves useful only when things must be kept safe but unused (παρακαταθέσ

lines.original: καὶ γὰρ γεωργία· ἢ οὔ;
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: ναί.
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: πρός γε καρποῦ κτῆσιν;
lines.english: Or like shoemaking for the acquisition of shoes,—that is what you mean?

lines.original: ναί.
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: καὶ μὴν καὶ σκυτοτομική;
lines.english: And what similar use or power of acquisition has justice in time of peace?

lines.original: ναί.
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: πρός γε ὑποδημάτων ἂν οἶμαι φαίης κτῆσιν;
lines.english: In contracts, Socrates, justice is of use.

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: And by contracts you mean partnerships?

lines.original: τί δὲ δή; τὴν δικαιοσύνην πρὸς τίνος χρείαν ἢ κτῆσιν ἐν εἰρήνῃ φαίης ἂν χρήσιμον εἶναι;
lines.english: Exactly.

lines.original: πρὸς τὰ συμβόλαια, ὦ Σώκρατες.
lines.english: But is the just man or the skilful player a more useful and better partner at a game of draughts?

lines.original: συμβόλαια δὲ λέγεις κοινωνήματα ἤ τι ἄλλο;
lines.english: The skilful player.

lines.original: κοινωνήματα δῆτα.
lines.english: And in the laying of bricks and stones is the just man a more useful or better partner than the builder?

lines.original: ἆρʼ οὖν ὁ δίκαιος ἀγαθὸς καὶ χρήσιμος κοινωνὸς εἰς πεττῶν θέσιν, ἢ ὁ πεττευτικός;
lines.english: Quite the reverse.

lines.original: ὁ πεττευτικός.
lines.english: Then in what sort of partnership is the just man a better partner than the harp-player, as in playing the harp the harp-player is certainly a better partner than the just man?

lines.original: ἀλλʼ εἰς πλίνθων καὶ λίθων θέσιν ὁ δίκαιος χρησιμώτερός τε καὶ ἀμείνων κοινωνὸς τοῦ οἰκοδομικοῦ;
lines.english: In a money partnership.

lines.original: οὐδαμῶς.
lines.english: Yes, Polemarchus, but surely not in the use of money; for you do not want a just man to be your counsellor in the purchase or sale of a horse; a man who is knowing about horses would be better for that, would he not?

lines.original: ἀλλʼ εἰς τίνα δὴ κοινωνίαν ὁ δίκαιος ἀμείνων κοινωνὸς τοῦ οἰκοδομικοῦ τε καὶ κιθαριστικοῦ, ὥσπερ ὁ κιθαριστικὸς τοῦ δικαίου εἰς κρουμάτων;
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: εἰς ἀργυρίου, ἔμοιγε δοκεῖ.
lines.english: And when you want to buy a ship, the shipwright or the pilot would be better?

lines.original: πλήν γʼ ἴσως, ὦ Πολέμαρχε, πρὸς τὸ χρῆσθαι ἀργυρίῳ, ὅταν δέῃ ἀργυρίου κοινῇ πρίασθαι ἢ ἀποδόσθαι ἵππον· τότεδέ, ὡς ἐγὼ οἶμαι, ὁ ἱππικός. ἦ γάρ;
lines.english: True.

lines.original: φαίνεται.
lines.english: Then what is that joint use of silver or gold in which the just man is to be preferred?

lines.original: καὶ μὴν ὅταν γε πλοῖον, ὁ ναυπηγὸς ἢ ὁ κυβερνήτης;
lines.english: When you want a deposit to be kept safely.

lines.original: ἔοικεν.
lines.english: You mean when money is not wanted, but allowed to lie?

lines.original: ὅταν οὖν τί δέῃ ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ κοινῇ χρῆσθαι, ὁ δίκαιος χρησιμώτερος τῶν ἄλλων;
lines.english: Precisely.

lines.original: ὅταν παρακαταθέσθαι καὶ σῶν εἶναι, ὦ Σώκρατες.
lines.english: That is to say, justice is useful when money is useless?

lines.original: οὐκοῦν λέγεις ὅταν μηδὲν δέῃ αὐτῷ χρῆσθαι ἀλλὰ κεῖσθαι;
lines.english: That is the inference.

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: And when you want to keep a pruning-hook safe, then justice is useful to the individual and to the state; but when you want to use it, then the art of the vine-dresser?

lines.original: ὅταν ἄρα ἄχρηστον ᾖ ἀργύριον, τότε χρήσιμος ἐπʼ αὐτῷἡ δικαιοσύνη;
lines.english: Clearly.

lines.original: κινδυνεύει.
lines.english: And when you want to keep a shield or a lyre, and not to use them, you would say that justice is useful; but when you want to use them, then the art of the soldier or of the musician?

lines.original: καὶ ὅταν δὴ δρέπανον δέῃ φυλάττειν, ἡ δικαιοσύνη χρήσιμος καὶ κοινῇ καὶ ἰδίᾳ· ὅταν δὲ χρῆσθαι, ἡ ἀμπελουργική;
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: φαίνεται.
lines.english: And so of all other things;—justice is useful when they are useless, and useless when they are useful?

lines.original: φήσεις δὲ καὶ ἀσπίδα καὶ λύραν ὅταν δέῃ φυλάττειν καὶ μηδὲν χρῆσθαι, χρήσιμον εἶναι τὴν δικαιοσύνην, ὅταν δὲ χρῆσθαι, τὴν ὁπλιτικὴν καὶ τὴν μουσικήν;
lines.english: That is the inference.

lines.original: ἀνάγκη.
lines.english: Then justice is not good for much.

lines.original: καὶ περὶ τἆλλα δὴ πάντα ἡ δικαιοσύνη ἑκάστου ἐν μὲν χρήσει ἄχρηστος, ἐν δὲ ἀχρηστίᾳ χρήσιμος;
lines.english: But let us consider this further point: Is not he who can best strike a blow in a boxing match or in any kind of fighting best able to ward off a blow?

lines.original: κινδυνεύει.
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: οὐκ ἂν οὖν, ὦ φίλε, πάνυ γέ τι σπουδαῖον εἴη ἡ δικαιοσύνη, εἰ πρὸς τὰ ἄχρηστα χρήσιμον ὂν τυγχάνει. τόδε δὲ σκεψώμεθα. ἆρʼ οὐχ ὁ πατάξαι δεινότατος ἐν μάχῃ εἴτε πυκτικῇ εἴτε τινὶ καὶ ἄλλῃ, οὗτος καὶ φυλάξασθαι;
lines.english: And he who is most skilful in preventing or escaping from a disease is best able to create one?

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: True.

lines.original: ἆρʼ οὖν καὶ νόσον ὅστις δεινὸς φυλάξασθαι, καὶ λαθεῖν οὗτος δεινότατος ἐμποιήσας;
lines.english: And he is the best guard of a camp who is best able to steal a march upon the enemy?

lines.original: ἔμοιγε δοκεῖ.
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: ἀνθρώπους κεκάσθαι κλεπτοσύνῃ θʼ ὅρκῳ τε Hom. Od. 19.395
lines.english: And so, you and Homer and Simonides are agreed that justice is an art of theft; to be practised however 'for the good of friends and for the harm of enemies,'—that was what you were saying?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

1. **κλεπτοσύνῃ** (dat. sg. fem.): "in thievery/stealing" - dative of respect
2. **φύλαξ** (nom. sg. masc.): "guardian" - subject complement  
3. **φὼρ** (nom. sg. masc.): "thief" - predicate nominative
4. **κλέπτης** (nom. sg. masc.): "thief/stealer" - predicate nominative
5. **ἀναπέφανται** (3rd sg. perf. mid./pass. indic.): "has been revealed" - from ἀναφαίνω
6. **διημαρτήκασιν** (3rd pl. perf. act. indic.): "have erred/made mistakes" - from διαμαρτάνω

**Gloss:**

Socrates develops a reductio argument: if the just person is skilled at guarding money, he must equally be skilled at stealing it, making justice a kind of "thievery for the benefit of friends," illustrated by Homer's praise of Autolycus who "excelled in thievery and oath-taking." The

lines.original: ἀλλὰ μὴν στρατοπέδου γε ὁ αὐτὸς φύλαξ ἀγαθός, ὅσπερ καὶ τὰ τῶν πολεμίων κλέψαι καὶ βουλεύματα καὶ τὰς ἄλλας πράξεις;
lines.english: And he is the best guard of a camp who is best able to steal a march upon the enemy?

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: ὅτου τις ἄρα δεινὸς φύλαξ, τούτου καὶ φὼρ δεινός.
lines.english: Then he who is a good keeper of anything is also a good thief?

lines.original: ἔοικεν.
lines.english: That, I suppose, is to be inferred.

lines.original: εἰ ἄρα ὁ δίκαιος ἀργύριον δεινὸς φυλάττειν, καὶ κλέπτειν δεινός.
lines.english: Then if the just man is good at keeping money, he is good at stealing it.

lines.original: ὡς γοῦν ὁ λόγος, ἔφη, σημαίνει.
lines.english: That is implied in the argument.

lines.original: κλέπτης ἄρα τις ὁ δίκαιος, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἀναπέφανται, καὶ κινδυνεύεις παρʼ Ὁμήρου μεμαθηκέναι αὐτό· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνοςτὸν τοῦ Ὀδυσσέως πρὸς μητρὸς πάππον Αὐτόλυκον ἀγαπᾷ τε καί φησιν αὐτὸν πάντας.
lines.english: Then after all the just man has turned out to be a thief. And this is a lesson which I suspect you must have learnt out of Homer; for he, speaking of Autolycus, the maternal grandfather of Odysseus, who is a favourite of his, affirms that 'He was excellent above all men in theft and perjury.'

lines.original: ἔοικεν οὖν ἡ δικαιοσύνη καὶ κατὰ σὲ καὶ καθʼ Ὅμηρον καὶ κατὰ Σιμωνίδην κλεπτική τις εἶναι, ἐπʼ ὠφελίᾳ μέντοι τῶν φίλων καὶ ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν ἐχθρῶν.
lines.english: And so, you and Homer and Simonides are agreed that justice is an art of theft; to be practised however 'for the good of friends and for the harm of enemies,'

lines.original: οὐχ οὕτως ἔλεγες;
lines.english: that was what you were saying?

lines.original: οὐ μὰ τὸν Δίʼ, ἔφη, ἀλλʼ οὐκέτι οἶδα ἔγωγε ὅτι ἔλεγον· τοῦτο μέντοι ἔμοιγε δοκεῖ ἔτι, ὠφελεῖν μὲν τοὺς φίλους ἡ δικαιοσύνη, βλάπτειν δὲ τοὺς ἐχθρούς.
lines.english: No, certainly not that, though I do not now know what I did say; but I still stand by the latter words.

lines.original: φίλους δὲ λέγεις εἶναι πότερον τοὺς δοκοῦντας ἑκάστῳ χρηστοὺς εἶναι, ἢ τοὺς ὄντας, κἂν μὴ δοκῶσι, καὶ ἐχθροὺς ὡσαύτως;
lines.english: Well, there is another question: By friends and enemies do we mean those who are so really, or only in seeming?

lines.original: εἰκὸς μέν, ἔφη, οὓς ἄν τις ἡγῆται χρηστοὺς φιλεῖν, οὓς δʼ ἂν πονηροὺς μισεῖν.
lines.english: Surely, he said, a man may be expected to love those whom he thinks good, and to hate those whom he thinks evil.

lines.original: ἆρʼ οὖν οὐχ ἁμαρτάνουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι περὶ τοῦτο, ὥστε δοκεῖν αὐτοῖς πολλοὺς μὲν χρηστοὺς εἶναι μὴ ὄντας, πολλοὺς δὲ τοὐναντίον;
lines.english: Yes, but do not persons often err about good and evil: many who are not good seem to be so, and conversely?

lines.original: ἁμαρτάνουσιν.
lines.english: That is true.

lines.original: τούτοις ἄρα οἱ μὲν ἀγαθοὶ ἐχθροί, οἱ δὲ κακοὶ φίλοι;
lines.english: Then to them the good will be enemies and the evil will be their friends?

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: True.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ὅμως δίκαιον τότε τούτοις τοὺς μὲν πονηροὺςὠφελεῖν, τοὺς δὲ ἀγαθοὺς βλάπτειν;
lines.english: And in that case they will be right in doing good to the evil and evil to the good?

lines.original: φαίνεται.
lines.english: Clearly.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ μὴν οἵ γε ἀγαθοὶ δίκαιοί τε καὶ οἷοι μὴ ἀδικεῖν;
lines.english: But the good are just and would not do an injustice?

lines.original: ἀληθῆ.
lines.english: True.

lines.original: κατὰ δὴ τὸν σὸν λόγον τοὺς μηδὲν ἀδικοῦντας δίκαιον κακῶς ποιεῖν.
lines.english: Then according to your argument it is just to injure those who do no wrong?

lines.original: μηδαμῶς, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες· πονηρὸς γὰρ ἔοικεν εἶναι ὁ λόγος.
lines.english: Nay, Socrates; the doctrine is immoral.

lines.original: τοὺς ἀδίκους ἄρα, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, δίκαιον βλάπτειν, τοὺς δὲ δικαίους ὠφελεῖν;
lines.english: Then I suppose that we ought to do good to the just and harm to the unjust?

lines.original: οὗτος ἐκείνου καλλίων φαίνεται.
lines.english: I like that better.

lines.original: πολλοῖς ἄρα, ὦ Πολέμαρχε, συμβήσεται, ὅσοι διημαρτήκασιντῶν ἀνθρώπων, δίκαιον εἶναι τοὺς μὲν φίλους βλάπτειν—πονηροὶ γὰρ αὐτοῖς εἰσιν—τοὺς δʼ ἐχθροὺς ὠφελεῖν —ἀγαθοὶ γάρ· καὶ οὕτως ἐροῦμεν αὐτὸ τοὐναντίον ἢ τὸν Σιμωνίδην ἔφαμεν λέγειν.
lines.english: But see the consequence:—Many a man who is ignorant of human nature has friends who are bad friends, and in that case he ought to do harm to them; and he has good enemies whom he ought to benefit; but, if so, we shall be saying the very opposite of that which we affirmed to be the meaning of Simonides.

lines.original: καὶ μάλα, ἔφη, οὕτω συμβαίνει. ἀλλὰ μεταθώμεθα· κινδυνεύομεν γὰρ οὐκ ὀρθῶς τὸν φίλον καὶ ἐχθρὸν θέσθαι.
lines.english: Very true, he said: and I think that we had better correct an error into which we seem to have fallen in the use of the words 'friend' and 'enemy.'

lines.original: πῶς θέμενοι, ὦ Πολέμαρχε;
lines.english: What was the error, Polemarchus? I asked.

lines.original: τὸν δοκοῦντα χρηστόν, τοῦτον φίλον εἶναι.
lines.english: We assumed that he is a friend who seems to be or who is thought good.

lines.original: νῦν δὲ πῶς, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, μεταθώμεθα;
lines.english: And how is the error to be corrected?

lines.original: τὸν δοκοῦντά τε, ἦ δʼ ὅς, καὶ τὸν ὄντα χρηστὸν φίλον·
lines.english: he is a friend who is, as well as seems, good;
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **τὸν δοκοῦντα** (acc. sing. masc. pres. act. ptc. of δοκέω): "the one seeming/appearing [to be]"
- **χρηστός** (nom. sing. masc. adj.): "good, worthy, useful"
- **βλάπτειν** (pres. act. inf. of βλάπτω): "to harm, injure"
- **ἀρετή** (nom. sing. fem.): "virtue, excellence"
- **δικαιοσύνη** (nom. sing. fem.): "justice, righteousness"
- **ὀφειλόμενα** (acc. pl. neut. pres. pass. ptc. of ὀφείλω): "things owed, what is due"

**Gloss:**

Socrates refines Polemarchus's definition of justice by distinguishing between those who merely seem good and those who truly are good friends. Through analogy with harm to horses and dogs (which makes them worse in their respective virtues), Socrates argues that justice, being human virtue, cannot have the work (ἔργον) of harming anyone, since har

lines.original: τὸν δὲ δοκοῦντα μέν, ὄντα δὲ μή, δοκεῖν ἀλλὰ μὴ εἶναι φίλον.
lines.english: and that he who seems only, and is not good, only seems to be and is not a friend;

lines.original: καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ δὲ ἡ αὐτὴ θέσις.
lines.english: and of an enemy the same may be said.

lines.original: φίλος μὲν δή, ὡς ἔοικε, τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἔσται, ἐχθρὸς δὲ ὁ πονηρός.
lines.english: You would argue that the good are our friends and the bad our enemies?

lines.original: ναί.
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: κελεύεις δὴ ἡμᾶς προσθεῖναι τῷ δικαίῳ ἢ ὡς τὸ πρῶτον ἐλέγομεν, λέγοντες δίκαιον εἶναι τὸν μὲν φίλον εὖ ποιεῖν, τὸν δʼ ἐχθρὸν κακῶς· νῦν πρὸς τούτῳ ὧδε λέγειν, ὅτι ἔστιν δίκαιον τὸν μὲν φίλον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα εὖ ποιεῖν, τὸν δʼ ἐχθρὸν κακὸν ὄντα βλάπτειν;
lines.english: And instead of saying simply as we did at first, that it is just to do good to our friends and harm to our enemies, we should further say: It is just to do good to our friends when they are good and harm to our enemies when they are evil?

lines.original: πάνυ μὲν οὖν, ἔφη, οὕτως ἄν μοι δοκεῖ καλῶς λέγεσθαι.
lines.english: Yes, that appears to me to be the truth.

lines.original: ἔστιν ἄρα, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, δικαίου ἀνδρὸς βλάπτειν καὶ ὁντινοῦν ἀνθρώπων;
lines.english: But ought the just to injure any one at all?

lines.original: καὶ πάνυ γε, ἔφη· τούς γε πονηρούς τε καὶ ἐχθροὺς δεῖ βλάπτειν.
lines.english: Undoubtedly he ought to injure those who are both wicked and his enemies.

lines.original: βλαπτόμενοι δʼ ἵπποι βελτίους ἢ χείρους γίγνονται;
lines.english: When horses are injured, are they improved or deteriorated?

lines.original: χείρους.
lines.english: The latter.

lines.original: ἆρα εἰς τὴν τῶν κυνῶν ἀρετήν, ἢ εἰς τὴν τῶν ἵππων;
lines.english: Deteriorated, that is to say, in the good qualities of horses, not of dogs?

lines.original: εἰς τὴν τῶν ἵππων.
lines.english: Yes, of horses.

lines.original: ἆρʼ οὖν καὶ κύνες βλαπτόμενοι χείρους γίγνονται εἰς τὴν τῶν κυνῶν ἀλλʼ οὐκ εἰς τὴν τῶν ἵππων ἀρετήν;
lines.english: And dogs are deteriorated in the good qualities of dogs, and not of horses?

lines.original: ἀνάγκη.
lines.english: Of course.

lines.original: ἀνθρώπους δέ, ὦ ἑταῖρε, μὴ οὕτω φῶμεν, βλαπτομένους εἰς τὴν ἀνθρωπείαν ἀρετὴν χείρους γίγνεσθαι;
lines.english: And will not men who are injured be deteriorated in that which is the proper virtue of man?

lines.original: πάνυ μὲν οὖν.
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ἡ δικαιοσύνη οὐκ ἀνθρωπεία ἀρετή;
lines.english: And that human virtue is justice?

lines.original: καὶ τοῦτʼ ἀνάγκη.
lines.english: To be sure.

lines.original: καὶ τοὺς βλαπτομένους ἄρα, ὦ φίλε, τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀνάγκη ἀδικωτέρους γίγνεσθαι.
lines.english: Then men who are injured are of necessity made unjust?

lines.original: ἔοικεν.
lines.english: That is the result.

lines.original: ἆρʼ οὖν τῇ μουσικῇ οἱ μουσικοὶ ἀμούσους δύνανται ποιεῖν;
lines.english: But can the musician by his art make men unmusical?

lines.original: ἀδύνατον.
lines.english: Certainly not.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ τῇ ἱππικῇ οἱ ἱππικοὶ ἀφίππους;
lines.english: Or the horseman by his art make them bad horsemen?

lines.original: οὐκ ἔστιν.
lines.english: Impossible.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ δὴ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀδίκους; ἢ καὶσυλλήβδην ἀρετῇ οἱ ἀγαθοὶ κακούς;
lines.english: And can the just by justice make men unjust, or speaking generally, can the good by virtue make them bad?

lines.original: ἀλλὰ ἀδύνατον.
lines.english: Assuredly not.

lines.original: οὐ γὰρ θερμότητος οἶμαι ἔργον ψύχειν ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐναντίου.
lines.english: Any more than heat can produce cold?

lines.original: ναί.
lines.english: It cannot.

lines.original: οὐδὲ ξηρότητος ὑγραίνειν ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐναντίου.
lines.english: Or drought moisture?

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: Clearly not.

lines.original: οὐδὲ δὴ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ βλάπτειν ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐναντίου.
lines.english: Nor can the good harm any one?

lines.original: φαίνεται.
lines.english: Impossible.

lines.original: ὁ δέ γε δίκαιος ἀγαθός;
lines.english: And the just is the good?

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: οὐκ ἄρα τοῦ δικαίου βλάπτειν ἔργον, ὦ Πολέμαρχε, οὔτε φίλον οὔτʼ ἄλλον οὐδένα, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐναντίου, τοῦ ἀδίκου.
lines.english: Then to injure a friend or any one else is not the act of a just man, but of the opposite, who is the unjust?

lines.original: παντάπασί μοι δοκεῖς ἀληθῆ λέγειν, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες.
lines.english: I think that what you say is quite true, Socrates.

lines.original: εἰ ἄρα τὰ ὀφειλόμενα ἑκάστῳ ἀποδιδόναι φησίν τις δίκαιον εἶναι, τοῦτο δὲ δὴ νοεῖ αὐτῷ τοῖς μὲν ἐχθροῖς βλάβην ὀφείλεσθαι παρὰ τοῦ δικαίου ἀνδρός, τοῖς δὲ φίλοις ὠφελίαν, οὐκ ἦν σοφὸς ὁ ταῦτα εἰπών. οὐ γὰρ ἀληθῆ ἔλεγεν· οὐδαμοῦ γὰρ δίκαιον οὐδένα ἡμῖν ἐφάνη ὂν βλάπτειν.
lines.english: Then if a man says that justice consists in the repayment of debts, and that good is the debt which a just man owes to his friends, and evil the debt which he owes to his enemies,—to say this is not wise; for it is not true, if, as has been clearly shown, the injuring of another can be in no case just.

lines.original: συγχωρῶ, ἦ δʼ ὅς.
lines.english: I agree with you, said Polemarchus.

lines.original: μαχούμεθα ἄρα, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, κοινῇ ἐγώ τε καὶ σύ, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ φῇ ἢ Σιμωνίδην ἢ Βίαντα ἢ Πιττακὸν εἰρηκέναι ἤ τινʼ ἄλλον τῶν σοφῶν τε καὶ μακαρίων ἀνδρῶν.
lines.english: Then you and I are prepared to take up arms against any one who attributes such a saying to Simonides or Bias or Pittacus, or any other wise man or seer?

lines.original: ἐγὼ γοῦν, ἔφη, ἕτοιμός εἰμι κοινωνεῖν τῆς μάχης.
lines.english: I am quite ready to do battle at your side, he said.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ οἶσθα, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, οὗ μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι τὸ ῥῆμα, τὸ φάναι δίκαιον εἶναι τοὺς μὲν φίλους ὠφελεῖν, τοὺς δʼ ἐχθροὺς βλάπτειν;
lines.english: Shall I tell you whose I believe the saying to be?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **ῥῆμα** (neuter accusative singular, noun): "saying" or "maxim"
- **ὠφελεῖν** (present active infinitive): "to benefit"
- **βλάπτειν** (present active infinitive): "to harm"
- **συστρέψας ἑαυτὸν** (aorist middle participle, nominative masculine singular): "gathering/coiling himself"
- **φλυαρία** (nominative singular, noun): "nonsense" or "idle talk"
- **ὑποκατακλινόμενοι** (present middle participle, nominative masculine plural): "yielding obsequiously to" or "fawning upon"

Socrates attributes the maxim about benefiting friends and harming enemies to tyrants and wealthy men who overestimate their power (Periander, Perdiccas, Xerxes, Ismenias). When Socrates asks what justice might be if not this definition, Thrasymachus—who had repeatedly tried to interrupt—finally bursts in like a wild beast, accusing Socrates and Polemarchus of indulging in nonsensical mutual flattery rather than earnestly seeking truth. Socrates

lines.original: τίνος;
lines.english: Whose?

lines.original: ἔφη.οἶμαι αὐτὸ Περιάνδρου εἶναι ἢ Περδίκκου ἢ Ξέρξου ἢ Ἰσμηνίου τοῦ Θηβαίου ἤ τινος ἄλλου μέγα οἰομένου δύνασθαι πλουσίου ἀνδρός.
lines.english: I believe that Periander or Perdiccas or Xerxes or Ismenias the Theban, or some other rich and mighty man, who had a great opinion of his own power, was the first to say that justice is 'doing good to your friends and harm to your enemies.'

lines.original: ἀληθέστατα, ἔφη, λέγεις.
lines.english: Most true, he said.

lines.original: εἶεν, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ· ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐδὲ τοῦτο ἐφάνη ἡ δικαιοσύνη ὂν οὐδὲ τὸ δίκαιον, τί ἂν ἄλλο τις αὐτὸ φαίη εἶναι;
lines.english: Yes, I said; but if this definition of justice also breaks down, what other can be offered?

lines.original: καὶ ὁ Θρασύμαχος πολλάκις μὲν καὶ διαλεγομένων ἡμῶν μεταξὺ ὥρμα ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι τοῦ λόγου, ἔπειτα ὑπὸ τῶν παρακαθημένων διεκωλύετο βουλομένων διακοῦσαι τὸν λόγον·
lines.english: Several times in the course of the discussion Thrasymachus had made an attempt to get the argument into his own hands, and had been put down by the rest of the company, who wanted to hear the end.

lines.original: ὡς δὲ διεπαυσάμεθα καὶ ἐγὼ ταῦτʼ εἶπον, οὐκέτι ἡσυχίαν ἦγεν, ἀλλὰ συστρέψας ἑαυτὸν ὥσπερ θηρίον ἧκεν ἐφʼ ἡμᾶς ὡς διαρπασόμενος.
lines.english: But when Polemarchus and I had done speaking and there was a pause, he could no longer hold his peace; and, gathering himself up, he came at us like a wild beast, seeking to devour us.

lines.original: καὶ ἐγώ τε καὶ ὁ Πολέμαρχος δείσαντες διεπτοήθημεν·
lines.english: We were quite panic-stricken at the sight of him.

lines.original: ὁ δʼ εἰς τὸ μέσον φθεγξάμενος, τίς, ἔφη, ὑμᾶς πάλαι φλυαρίαἔχει, ὦ Σώκρατες;
lines.english: He roared out to the whole company: What folly, Socrates, has taken possession of you all?

lines.original: καὶ τί εὐηθίζεσθε πρὸς ἀλλήλους ὑποκατακλινόμενοι ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς;
lines.english: And why, sillybillies, do you knock under to one another?

lines.original: ἀλλʼ εἴπερ ὡς ἀληθῶς βούλει εἰδέναι τὸ δίκαιον ὅτι ἔστι, μὴ μόνον ἐρώτα μηδὲ φιλοτιμοῦ ἐλέγχων ἐπειδάν τίς τι ἀποκρίνηται, ἐγνωκὼς τοῦτο, ὅτι ῥᾷον ἐρωτᾶν ἢ ἀποκρίνεσθαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς ἀπόκριναι καὶ εἰπὲ τί φῂς εἶναι τὸ δίκαιον.
lines.english: I say that if you want really to know what justice is, you should not only ask but answer, and you should not seek honour to yourself from the refutation of an opponent, but have your own answer; for there is many a one who can ask and cannot answer.

lines.original: καὶ ὅπως μοι μὴ ἐρεῖς ὅτι τὸδέον ἐστὶν μηδʼ ὅτι τὸ ὠφέλιμον μηδʼ ὅτι τὸ λυσιτελοῦν μηδʼ ὅτι τὸ κερδαλέον μηδʼ ὅτι τὸ συμφέρον, ἀλλὰ σαφῶς μοι καὶ ἀκριβῶς λέγε ὅτι ἂν λέγῃς·
lines.english: And now I will not have you say that justice is duty or advantage or profit or gain or interest, for this sort of nonsense will not do for me; I must have clearness and accuracy.

lines.original: ὡς ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀποδέξομαι ἐὰν ὕθλους τοιούτους λέγῃς.
καὶ ἐγὼ ἀκούσας ἐξεπλάγην καὶ προσβλέπων αὐτὸν ἐφοβούμην, καί μοι δοκῶ, εἰ μὴ πρότερος ἑωράκη αὐτὸν ἢ ἐκεῖνος ἐμέ, ἄφωνος ἂν γενέσθαι.
lines.english: I was panic-stricken at his words, and could not look at him without trembling. Indeed I believe that if I had not fixed my eye upon him, I should have been struck dumb:

lines.original: νῦν δὲ ἡνίκα ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἤρχετο ἐξαγριαίνεσθαι, προσέβλεψα αὐτὸν πρότερος,ὥστε αὐτῷ οἷός τʼ ἐγενόμην ἀποκρίνασθαι, καὶ εἶπον ὑποτρέμων·
lines.english: but when I saw his fury rising, I looked at him first, and was therefore able to reply to him.

lines.original: ὦ Θρασύμαχε, μὴ χαλεπὸς ἡμῖν ἴσθι·
lines.english: Thrasymachus, I said, with a quiver, don't be hard upon us.

lines.original: εἰ γάρ τι ἐξαμαρτάνομεν ἐν τῇ τῶν λόγων σκέψει ἐγώ τε καὶ ὅδε, εὖ ἴσθι ὅτι ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνομεν.
lines.english: Polemarchus and I may have been guilty of a little mistake in the argument, but I can assure you that the error was not intentional.

lines.original: μὴ γὰρ δὴ οἴου, εἰ μὲν χρυσίον ἐζητοῦμεν, οὐκ ἄν ποτε ἡμᾶς ἑκόντας εἶναι ὑποκατακλίνεσθαι ἀλλήλοις ἐν τῇ ζητήσει καὶ διαφθείρειν τὴν εὕρεσιν αὐτοῦ, δικαιοσύνην δὲ ζητοῦντας, πρᾶγμα πολλῶν χρυσίων τιμιώτερον, ἔπειθʼ οὕτως ἀνοήτως ὑπείκειν ἀλλήλοις καὶ οὐ σπουδάζειν ὅτι μάλιστα φανῆναι αὐτό.
lines.english: If we were seeking for a piece of gold, you would not imagine that we were 'knocking under to one another,' and so losing our chance of finding it. And why, when we are seeking for justice, a thing more precious than many pieces of gold, do you say that we are weakly yielding to one another and not doing our utmost to get at the truth? Nay, my good friend, we are most willing and anxious to do so, but the fact is that we cannot.

lines.original: ὅπως μοι, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, μὴ ἐρεῖς ὅτι ἔστιν τὰ δώδεκα δὶς ἓξ μηδʼ ὅτι τρὶς τέτταρα μηδʼ ὅτι ἑξάκις δύο μηδʼ ὅτι τετράκις τρία·
lines.english: I say that if you want really to know what justice is, you should not only ask but answer, and you should not seek honour to yourself from the refutation of an opponent, but have your own answer; for there is many a one who can ask and cannot answer. And now I will not have you say that justice is duty or advantage or profit or gain or interest, for this sort of nonsense will not do for me; I must have clearness and accuracy.
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **φλυαρῇς** (verb, 2nd sg. pres. subj. act.): "you might babble/talk nonsense"
- **ἀνεκάγχασέ** (verb, 3rd sg. aor. ind. act.): "he burst out laughing"
- **σαρδάνιον** (adv.): "sardonically/scornfully"
- **εἰρωνεία** (noun, nom. sg. fem.): "habitual irony/dissembling"
- **διαπράξηται** (verb, 3rd sg. aor. subj. mid.): "he might accomplish/carry out"

Thrasymachus sarcastically demands that Socrates not give trivial mathematical variations as his answer about justice (like saying twelve equals six times two, etc.). When Socrates protests that such restrictions make answering difficult, Thrasymachus bursts into scornful laughter, calling out Socrates' "habitual irony" and predicting he will refuse to answer directly but instead cross-examine others. The exchange dramatizes their methodological conflict, with Thrasymachus mocking Socrates' elenctic technique.

lines.original: ὡς οὐκ ἀποδέξομαί σου ἐὰν τοιαῦτα φλυαρῇς ὦ Θρασύμαχε, πῶς λέγεις;
lines.english: You are a philosopher, Thrasymachus, I replied, and well know that if you ask a person what numbers make up twelve, taking care to prohibit him whom you ask from answering twice six, or three times four, or six times two, or four times three, 'for this sort of nonsense will not do for me,'—then obviously, if that is your way of putting the question, no one can answer you.

lines.original: μὴ ἀποκρίνωμαι ὧν προεῖπες μηδέν;
lines.english: But suppose that he were to retort, 'Thrasymachus, what do you mean?

lines.original: πότερον, ὦ θαυμάσιε, μηδʼ εἰ τούτων τι τυγχάνει ὄν, ἀλλʼ ἕτερον εἴπω τιτοῦ ἀληθοῦς;
lines.english: If one of these numbers which you interdict be the true answer to the question, am I falsely to say some other number which is not the right one?—is that your meaning?'

lines.original: ἢ πῶς λέγεις;
lines.english: How would you answer him?

lines.original: οἴου γε σύ, ὦ φίλε.
lines.english: Just as if the two cases were at all alike! he said.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ οἶμαι οὐ δυνάμεθα·
lines.english: Why should they not be? I replied; and even if they are not, but only appear to be so to the person who is asked, ought he not to say what he thinks, whether you and I forbid him or not?

lines.original: ἐλεεῖσθαι οὖν ἡμᾶς πολὺμᾶλλον εἰκός ἐστίν που ὑπὸ ὑμῶν τῶν δεινῶν ἢ χαλεπαίνεσθαι.
lines.english: I presume then that you are going to make one of the interdicted answers?

lines.original: καὶ ὃς ἀκούσας ἀνεκάγχασέ τε μάλα σαρδάνιον καὶ εἶπεν·
lines.english: I dare say that I may, notwithstanding the danger, if upon reflection I approve of any of them.

lines.original: ὦ Ἡράκλεις, ἔφη, αὕτη ʼκείνη ἡ εἰωθυῖα εἰρωνεία Σωκράτους, καὶ ταῦτʼ ἐγὼ ᾔδη τε καὶ τούτοις προύλεγον, ὅτι σὺ ἀποκρίνασθαι μὲν οὐκ ἐθελήσοις, εἰρωνεύσοιο δὲ καὶ πάντα μᾶλλον ποιήσοις ἢ ἀποκρινοῖο, εἴ τίς τί σε ἐρωτᾷ.
lines.english: But what if I give you an answer about justice other and better, he said, than any of these? What do you deserve to have done to you?

lines.original: σοφὸς γὰρ εἶ, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ὦ Θρασύμαχε·
lines.english: Done to me!—as becomes the ignorant, I must learn from the wise—that is what I deserve to have done to me.

lines.original: εὖ οὖν ᾔδησθα ὅτι εἴ τινα ἔροιο ὁπόσα ἐστὶν τὰ δώδεκα, καὶ ἐρόμενος προείποιςαὐτῷ——δῆλον οἶμαί σοι ἦν ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἀποκρινοῖτο τῷ οὕτως πυνθανομένῳ.
lines.english: What, and no payment! a pleasant notion!

lines.original: ἀλλʼ εἴ σοι εἶπεν·τί ἂν αὐτῷ εἶπες πρὸς ταῦτα;
lines.english: I will pay when I have the money, I replied.

lines.original: εἶεν, ἔφη·
lines.english: But you have, Socrates, said Glaucon: and you, Thrasymachus, need be under no anxiety about money, for we will all make a contribution for Socrates.

lines.original: ὡς δὴ ὅμοιον τοῦτο ἐκείνῳ.
lines.english: Yes, he replied, and then Socrates will do as he always does—refuse to answer himself, but take and pull to pieces the answer of some one else.

lines.original: οὐδέν γε κωλύει, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ·
lines.english: Why, my good friend, I said, how can any one answer who knows, and says that he knows, just nothing; and who, even if he has some faint notions of his own, is told by a man of authority not to utter them?

lines.original: εἰ δʼ οὖν καὶ μὴ ἔστιν ὅμοιον, φαίνεται δὲ τῷ ἐρωτηθέντι τοιοῦτον, ἧττόν τι αὐτὸν οἴει ἀποκρινεῖσθαι τὸ φαινόμενον ἑαυτῷ, ἐάντε ἡμεῖς ἀπαγορεύωμεν ἐάντε μή;
lines.english: The natural thing is, that the speaker should be some one like yourself who professes to know and can tell what he knows. Will you then kindly answer, for the edification of the company and of myself?

lines.original: ἄλλο τι οὖν, ἔφη, καὶ σὺ οὕτω ποιήσεις;
lines.english: Glaucon and the rest of the company joined in my request, and Thrasymachus, as any one might see, was in reality eager to speak; for he thought that he had an excellent answer, and would distinguish himself.

lines.original: ὧν ἐγὼ ἀπεῖπον, τούτων τι ἀποκρινῇ;
lines.english: But at first he affected to insist on my answering; at length he consented to begin.

lines.original: οὐκ ἂν θαυμάσαιμι, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ·
lines.english: Behold, he said, the wisdom of Socrates; he refuses to teach himself, and goes about learning of others, to whom he never even says Thank you.

lines.original: εἴ μοι σκεψαμένῳ οὕτω δόξειεν.
lines.english: That I learn of others, I replied, is quite true; but that I am ungrateful I wholly deny.

lines.original: τί οὖν, ἔφη, ἂν ἐγὼ δείξω ἑτέραν ἀπόκρισιν παρὰ πάσας ταύτας περὶ δικαιοσύνης, βελτίω τούτων;
lines.english: Money I have none, and therefore I pay in praise, which is all I have; and how ready I am to praise any one who appears to me to speak well you will very soon find out when you answer; for I expect that you will answer well.

lines.original: τί ἀξιοῖς παθεῖν;
lines.english: Listen, then, he said; I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.

lines.original: τί ἄλλο, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ἢ ὅπερ προσήκει πάσχειν τῷ μὴ εἰδότι;
lines.english: And now why do you not praise me? But of course you won't.

lines.original: προσήκει δέ που μαθεῖν παρὰ τοῦ εἰδότος·
lines.english: Let me first understand you, I replied.

lines.original: καὶ ἐγὼ οὖν τοῦτο ἀξιῶ παθεῖν.
lines.english: Justice, as you say, is the interest of the stronger.

lines.original: ἡδὺς γὰρ εἶ, ἔφη·
lines.english: What, Thrasymachus, is the meaning of this?

lines.original: ἀλλὰ πρὸς τῷ μαθεῖν καὶ ἀπότεισον ἀργύριον.
lines.english: You cannot mean to say that because Polydamas, the pancratiast, is stronger than we are, and finds the eating of beef conducive to his bodily strength, that to eat beef is therefore equally for our good who are weaker than he is, and right and just for us?

lines.original: οὐκοῦν ἐπειδάν μοι γένηται, εἶπον.
lines.english: That's abominable of you, Socrates; you take the words in the sense which is most damaging to the argument.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ἔστιν, ἔφη ὁ Γλαύκων.
lines.english: Not at all, my good sir, I said; I am trying to understand them; and I wish that you would be a little clearer.

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ἕνεκα ἀργυρίου, ὦ Θρασύμαχε, λέγε·
lines.english: Well, he said, have you never heard that forms of government differ; there are tyrannies, and there are democracies, and there are aristocracies?

lines.original: πάντες γὰρ ἡμεῖς Σωκράτει εἰσοίσομεν.
lines.english: Yes, I know.

lines.original: πάνυ γε οἶμαι, ἦ δʼ ὅς·
lines.english: And the government is the ruling power in each state?

lines.original: ἵνα Σωκράτης τὸ εἰωθὸς διαπράξηται·
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: αὐτὸς μὲν μὴ ἀποκρίνηται, ἄλλου δʼ ἀποκρινομένου λαμβάνῃ λόγον καὶ ἐλέγχῃ.
lines.english: And the different forms of government make laws democratical, aristocratical, tyrannical, with a view to their several interests; and these laws, which are made by them for their own interests, are the justice which they deliver to their subjects, and him who transgresses them they punish as a breaker of the law, and unjust. And that is what I mean when I say that in all states there is the same principle of justice, which is the interest of the government; and as the government must be supposed to have power, the only reasonable conclusion is, that everywhere there is one principle of justice, which is the interest of the stronger.

lines.original: πῶς γὰρ ἄν, ἔφην ἐγώ, ὦ βέλτιστε, τὶς ἀποκρίναιτο πρῶτον μὲν μὴ εἰδὼς μηδὲ φάσκων εἰδέναι, ἔπειτα, εἴ τι καὶ οἴεται, περὶ τούτων ἀπειρημένον αὐτῷ εἴη ὅπως μηδὲν ἐρεῖ ὧν ἡγεῖται ὑπʼ ἀνδρὸς οὐ φαύλου;
lines.english: Why, my good friend, I said, how can any one answer who knows, and says that he knows, just nothing; and who, even if he has some faint notions of his own, is told by a man of authority not to utter them?
lines.gloss:
**Key Terms:**

- **ἀποκρίναιτο** (ἀποκρίνομαι): 3rd sing. aor. mid. opt., "answer, reply"
- **ἀπειρημένον** (ἀπερέω): perf. pass. part. nom./acc. sing. neut., "forbidden, prohibited"
- **τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον**: articular phrase, "the advantage of the stronger" (τοῦ κρείττονος = gen. sing. comparative)
- **τίθεται** (τίθημι): 3rd sing. pres. mid. indic., "establishes, lays down"
- **ἑκάστη ἡ ἀρχὴ**: nom. sing., "each regime/ruling power"
- **ἐκβαίνοντα** (ἐκβαίνω): pres. act. part. acc. sing. masc., "transgressing, departing from"

**Gloss:**

Socrates protests that answering under Thrasymachus' restrictive conditions is impossible, urging him instead to state his

lines.original: ἀλλὰ σὲ δὴ μᾶλλονεἰκὸς λέγειν· σὺ γὰρ δὴ φῂς εἰδέναι καὶ ἔχειν εἰπεῖν.
lines.english: The natural thing is, that the speaker should be some one like yourself who professes to know and can tell what he knows.

lines.original: μὴ οὖν ἄλλως ποίει, ἀλλὰ ἐμοί τε χαρίζου ἀποκρινόμενος καὶ μὴ φθονήσῃς καὶ Γλαύκωνα τόνδε διδάξαι καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους.
lines.english: Will you then kindly answer, for the edification of the company and of myself?

lines.original: εἰπόντος δέ μου ταῦτα, ὅ τε Γλαύκων καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι ἐδέοντο αὐτοῦ μὴ ἄλλως ποιεῖν.
lines.english: Glaucon and the rest of the company joined in my request, and Thrasymachus, as any one might see, was in reality eager to speak;

lines.original: καὶ ὁ Θρασύμαχος φανερὸς μὲν ἦν ἐπιθυμῶν εἰπεῖν ἵνʼ εὐδοκιμήσειεν, ἡγούμενος ἔχειν ἀπόκρισιν παγκάλην· προσεποιεῖτο δὲ φιλονικεῖν πρὸς τὸ ἐμὲ εἶναι τὸν ἀποκρινόμενον.
lines.english: for he thought that he had an excellent answer, and would distinguish himself. But at first he affected to insist on my answering;

lines.original: τελευτῶν δὲ συνεχώρησεν,κἄπειτα, αὕτη δή, ἔφη, ἡ Σωκράτους σοφία· αὐτὸν μὲν μὴ ἐθέλειν διδάσκειν, παρὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων περιιόντα μανθάνειν καὶ τούτων μηδὲ χάριν ἀποδιδόναι.
lines.english: at length he consented to begin. Behold, he said, the wisdom of Socrates; he refuses to teach himself, and goes about learning of others, to whom he never even says Thank you.

lines.original: ὅτι μέν, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, μανθάνω παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων, ἀληθῆ εἶπες, ὦ Θρασύμαχε, ὅτι δὲ οὔ με φῂς χάριν ἐκτίνειν, ψεύδῃ· ἐκτίνω γὰρ ὅσην δύναμαι.
lines.english: That I learn of others, I replied, is quite true; but that I am ungrateful I wholly deny.

lines.original: δύναμαι δὲ ἐπαινεῖν μόνον· χρήματα γὰρ οὐκ ἔχω.
lines.english: Money I have none, and therefore I pay in praise, which is all I have;

lines.original: ὡς δὲ προθύμως τοῦτο δρῶ, ἐάν τίς μοι δοκῇ εὖ λέγειν, εὖ εἴσῃ αὐτίκα δὴ μάλα, ἐπειδὰν ἀποκρίνῃ· οἶμαι γάρ σε εὖ ἐρεῖν.
lines.english: and how ready I am to praise any one who appears to me to speak well you will very soon find out when you answer; for I expect that you will answer well.

lines.original: ἄκουε δή, ἦ δʼ ὅς.
lines.english: Listen, then, he said;

lines.original: φημὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἶναι τὸ δίκαιον οὐκ ἄλλο τι ἢ τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον.
lines.english: I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.

lines.original: ἀλλὰ τί οὐκ ἐπαινεῖς;
lines.english: And now why do you not praise me?

lines.original: ἀλλʼ οὐκ ἐθελήσεις.
lines.english: But of course you won't.

lines.original: ἐὰν μάθω γε πρῶτον, ἔφην, τί λέγεις· νῦν γὰρ οὔπω οἶδα.
lines.english: Let me first understand you, I replied.

lines.original: τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος φῂς συμφέρον δίκαιον εἶναι.
lines.english: Justice, as you say, is the interest of the stronger.

lines.original: καὶ τοῦτο, ὦ Θρασύμαχε, τί ποτε λέγεις;
lines.english: What, Thrasymachus, is the meaning of this?

lines.original: οὐ γάρ που τό γε τοιόνδε φῄς· εἰ Πουλυδάμας ἡμῶν κρείττων ὁ παγκρατιαστὴς καὶ αὐτῷ συμφέρει τὰ βόεια κρέα πρὸς τὸ σῶμα, τοῦτο τὸσιτίον εἶναι καὶ ἡμῖν τοῖς ἥττοσιν ἐκείνου συμφέρον ἅμα καὶ δίκαιον.
lines.english: You cannot mean to say that because Polydamas, the pancratiast, is stronger than we are, and finds the eating of beef conducive to his bodily strength, that to eat beef is therefore equally for our good who are weaker than he is, and right and just for us?

lines.original: βδελυρὸς γὰρ εἶ, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες, καὶ ταύτῃ ὑπολαμβάνεις ᾗ ἂν κακουργήσαις μάλιστα τὸν λόγον.
lines.english: That's abominable of you, Socrates; you take the words in the sense which is most damaging to the argument.

lines.original: εἶτʼ οὐκ οἶσθʼ, ἔφη, ὅτι τῶν πόλεων αἱ μὲν τυραννοῦνται, αἱ δὲ δημοκρατοῦνται, αἱ δὲ ἀριστοκρατοῦνται;
lines.english: Well, he said, have you never heard that forms of government differ; there are tyrannies, and there are democracies, and there are aristocracies?

lines.original: πῶς γὰρ οὔ;
lines.english: Yes, I know.

lines.original: οὐκοῦν τοῦτο κρατεῖ ἐν ἑκάστῃ πόλει, τὸ ἄρχον;
lines.english: And the government is the ruling power in each state?

lines.original: πάνυ γε.
lines.english: Certainly.

lines.original: τίθεται δέ γε τοὺς νόμους ἑκάστη ἡ ἀρχὴ πρὸς τὸ αὑτῇ συμφέρον, δημοκρατία μὲν δημοκρατικούς, τυραννὶς δὲ τυραννικούς, καὶ αἱ ἄλλαι οὕτως· θέμεναι δὲ ἀπέφηναν τοῦτο δίκαιον τοῖς ἀρχομένοις εἶναι, τὸ σφίσι συμφέρον, καὶ τὸν τούτου ἐκβαίνοντα κολάζουσιν ὡς παρανομοῦντά τε καὶ ἀδικοῦντα.
lines.english: And the different forms of government make laws democratical, aristocratical, tyrannical, with a view to their several interests; and these laws, which are made by them for their own interests, are the justice which they deliver to their subjects, and him who transgresses them they punish as a breaker of the law, and unjust.

lines.original: τοῦ κρείττονος.
lines.english: the interest of the stronger.
lines.gloss:
**Key terms:** 

- **καθεστηκυίας ἀρχῆς** (fem. gen. sg. perfect participle + gen. sg. noun): "of the established government/ruling power"
- **κρατεῖ** (3rd sg. present active): "it holds power, rules"
- **ἀναμάρτητοι** (nom. pl. masc. adjective): "infallible, incapable of error"
- **ἁμαρτεῖν** (aorist active infinitive): "to make mistakes, to err"
- **ἀσύμφορα** (acc. pl. neut. adjective): "disadvantageous things, what is not beneficial"

Thrasymachus asserts that justice in all cities is the advantage of the established ruling power, which holds control. Socrates secures agreement that obedience to rulers is just, then asks whether rulers are infallible or capable of error. Through a series of concessions, Socrates demonstrates that if rulers can mistakenly legislate what is disadvantageous to themselves, and if subjects must justly obey such laws, then justice would sometimes require doing what is disadvantageous to the stronger—the opposite of Thrasymachus's definition.

lines.original: τοῦτʼ οὖν ἐστιν, ὦ βέλτιστε, ὃ λέγω ἐν ἁπάσαιςταῖς πόλεσιν ταὐτὸν εἶναι δίκαιον, τὸ τῆς καθεστηκυίας ἀρχῆς συμφέρον·
lines.english: And that is what I mean when I say that in all states there is the same principle of justice, which is the interest of the government;

lines.original: αὕτη δέ που κρατεῖ, ὥστε συμβαίνει τῷ ὀρθῶς λογιζομένῳ πανταχοῦ εἶναι τὸ αὐτὸ δίκαιον, τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον.
lines.english: and as the government must be supposed to have power, the only reasonable conclusion is, that everywhere there is one principle of justice, which is the interest of the stronger.

lines.original: νῦν, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ἔμαθον ὃ λέγεις·
lines.english: Now I understand you, I said;

lines.original: εἰ δὲ ἀληθὲς ἢ μή, πειράσομαι μαθεῖν.
lines.english: and whether you are right or not I will try to discover.

lines.original: τὸ συμφέρον μὲν οὖν, ὦ Θρασύμαχε, καὶ σὺ ἀπεκρίνω δίκαιον εἶναι—καίτοι ἔμοιγε ἀπηγόρευες ὅπως μὴ τοῦτο ἀποκρινοίμην—πρόσεστιν δὲ δὴ αὐτόθι τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος.
lines.english: But let me remark, that in defining justice you have yourself used the word 'interest' which you forbade me to use. It is true, however, that in your definition the words 'of the stronger' are added.

lines.original: σμικρά γε ἴσως, ἔφη, προσθήκη.
lines.english: A small addition, you must allow, he said.

lines.original: οὔπω δῆλον οὐδʼ εἰ μεγάλη·
lines.english: Great or small, never mind about that:

lines.original: ἀλλʼ ὅτι μὲν τοῦτο σκεπτέον εἰ ἀληθῆ λέγεις, δῆλον.
lines.english: we must first enquire whether what you are saying is the truth.

lines.original: ἐπειδὴ γὰρ συμφέρον γέ τι εἶναι καὶ ἐγὼ ὁμολογῶ τὸ δίκαιον, σὺ δὲ προστιθεῖς καὶ αὐτὸ φῂς εἶναι τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγνοῶ, σκεπτέον δή.
lines.english: Now we are both agreed that justice is interest of some sort, but you go on to say 'of the stronger'; about this addition I am not so sure, and must therefore consider further.

lines.original: σκόπει, ἔφη.
lines.english: Proceed.

lines.original: ταῦτʼ ἔσται, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ.
lines.english: I will; and first tell me,

lines.original: καί μοι εἰπέ· οὐ καὶ πείθεσθαι μέντοι τοῖς ἄρχουσιν δίκαιον φῂς εἶναι;
lines.english: Do you admit that it is just for subjects to obey their rulers?

lines.original: ἔγωγε.
lines.english: I do.

lines.original: πότερον δὲ ἀναμάρτητοί εἰσιν οἱ ἄρχοντες ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν ἑκάσταις ἢ οἷοί τι καὶ ἁμαρτεῖν;
lines.english: But are the rulers of states absolutely infallible, or are they sometimes liable to err?

lines.original: πάντως που, ἔφη, οἷοί τι καὶ ἁμαρτεῖν.
lines.english: To be sure, he replied, they are liable to err.

lines.original: οὐκοῦν ἐπιχειροῦντες νόμους τιθέναι τοὺς μὲν ὀρθῶς τιθέασιν, τοὺς δέ τινας οὐκ ὀρθῶς;
lines.english: Then in making their laws they may sometimes make them rightly, and sometimes not?

lines.original: οἶμαι ἔγωγε.
lines.english: True.

lines.original: τὸ δὲ ὀρθῶς ἆρα τὸ τὰ συμφέροντά ἐστι τίθεσθαι ἑαυτοῖς, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὀρθῶς ἀσύμφορα;
lines.english: When they make them rightly, they make them agreeably to their interest; when they are mistaken, contrary to their interest;

lines.original: ἢ πῶς λέγεις;
lines.english: you admit that?

lines.original: οὕτως.
lines.english: Yes.

lines.original: ἃ δʼ ἂν θῶνται ποιητέον τοῖς ἀρχομένοις, καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ δίκαιον;
lines.english: And the laws which they make must be obeyed by their subjects,—and that is what you call justice?

lines.original: πῶς γὰρ οὔ;
lines.english: Doubtless.

lines.original: οὐ μόνον ἄρα δίκαιόν ἐστιν κατὰ τὸν σὸν λόγον τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον ποιεῖν ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὐναντίον, τὸ μὴ συμφέρον.
lines.english: Then justice, according to your argument, is not only obedience to the interest of the stronger but the reverse?

lines.original: τί λέγεις σύ;
lines.english: What is that you are saying?

lines.original: ἔφη.
lines.english: he asked.

lines.original: ἃ σὺ λέγεις, ἔμοιγε δοκῶ·
lines.english: I am only repeating what you are saying, I believe.

lines.original: σκοπῶμεν δὲ βέλτιον.
lines.english: But let us consider:

lines.original: οὐχ ὡμολόγηται τοὺς ἄρχοντας τοῖς ἀρχομένοις προστάττοντας ποιεῖν ἄττα ἐνίοτε διαμαρτάνειν τοῦ ἑαυτοῖς βελτίστου, ἃ δʼ ἂν προστάττωσιν οἱ ἄρχοντες δίκαιον εἶναι τοῖς ἀρχομένοις ποιεῖν;
lines.english: Have we not admitted that the rulers may be mistaken about their own interest in what they command, and also that to obey them is justice?

lines.original: ταῦτʼ οὐχ ὡμολόγηται;
lines.english: Has not that been admitted?

lines.original: οἶμαι ἔγωγε, ἔφη.
lines.english: Yes.
